source.version: arXiv:2609.15472v1, 14 September 2026; ACII 2026 conference-formatted preprint, including Supplementary Material (Appendices A-I).
source.title_on_document: Spook the Machine: Gamified Exploration of Human Imagination of Machine Fear

supplement.where: PDF pp. 11-18, Supplementary Material, Appendices A-I.
supplement.holds: Thematic overview; gallery-context robustness of prompt predictability (Figure 8); interface and architecture; analysis implementation; scoring algorithm, including explicit machine-level randomization; LLM prompts and emotional-reaction prompts. No per-arm person counts or post-exclusion person count is stated.

paper_design_summary: Public visitors generated images with FLUX.1 or uploaded images to frighten GPT-4o-based machines, under scoring rules rewarding spookiness alone or spookiness plus novelty, crossed with neutral or high-emotion feedback. Machines were randomized to scoring rules, participants selected machines, and emotional feedback flipped after five successful scares; this does not establish random assignment of people or condition order (pp. 3-4, Sections IV.B-E; p. 13, Appendix F.D; p. 7, Section VI). Analyses scored fear relevance and convergence of prompts and images, with 832 unique platform participants reported but no distinct-person count after record exclusions (pp. 4-6, Sections IV.E-F and V).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each machine received one cell of the scoring-rule by emotional-condition factorial design at creation. The supplement explicitly randomizes machines to spookiness-only or combined spookiness-and-uncertainty scoring; it does not state random assignment of people. Participants selected a machine. Emotional condition flipped after five successful scares, introducing success-dependent within-person exposure; random assignment of its initial state or order is not stated.
assignment.quote: Participants select a machine and either enter a prompt to generate an image via FLUX.1 [50] or upload an image.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section IV.C (participant choice) and IV.B (emotion switches); p. 4, Section IV.E (machine-level factorial cells); p. 13, Appendix F.D (random scoring-rule assignment to machines); p. 7, Section VI (success-confounded within-person variation).

arms.name: Spookiness-only / neutral
arms.description: Machine initially uses spookiness-only scoring and neutral emotional reactions; visitors may generate images with FLUX.1 or upload images. Emotion can switch after successful scares. People counts are not reported by cell (pp. 3-4, Sections IV.B-E).

arms.name: Spookiness-only / high-emotion
arms.description: Machine initially uses spookiness-only scoring and high-emotion reactions; visitors may generate images with FLUX.1 or upload images. Emotion can switch after successful scares. People counts are not reported by cell (pp. 3-4, Sections IV.B-E).

arms.name: Combined / neutral
arms.description: Machine initially rewards spookiness plus uncertainty (novelty) and uses neutral emotional reactions; visitors may generate images with FLUX.1 or upload images. Emotion can switch after successful scares. People counts are not reported by cell (pp. 3-4, Sections IV.B-E).

arms.name: Combined / high-emotion
arms.description: Machine initially rewards spookiness plus uncertainty (novelty) and uses high-emotion reactions; visitors may generate images with FLUX.1 or upload images. Emotion can switch after successful scares. People counts are not reported by cell (pp. 3-4, Sections IV.B-E).

participants.exclusions: Before analysis, the authors removed prelaunch test submissions, incomplete records missing prompt text, score or condition assignment, and a small number of inappropriate submissions that bypassed automated filtering and were identified by keyword matching (p. 4, Section IV.F). The Ethical Impact Statement also reports automated keyword filtering and manual review (p. 7). These are record exclusions; exact excluded-person and final distinct-person analysis counts are not reported. The randomized and analyzed people counts remain null.
participants.who: Self-selected public website visitors recruited organically through media coverage and Hacker News; no demographics collected. The paper reports 832 unique platform participants interacting with 89 machines and producing 15,719 artifacts, of which 7,650 were scored. It describes exclusions of records before analysis but does not state the remaining number of distinct people or people per condition, so n_analyzed is null.
participants.quote: Over this period, 832 unique participants interacted with 89 machines and produced 15,719 artifacts, of which 7,650 received a score;
participants.locator: p. 4, Section IV.E (deployment counts and recruitment), Section IV.F (record exclusions); p. 7, Ethical Impact Statement (keyword filtering and manual review); p. 8, Ethical Impact Statement (self-selected public sample and no demographics). Supplementary Material, pp. 11-18, gives no post-exclusion person count.

ai_tool.name_model: FLUX.1 (image generation); GPT-4o (machine characterization, image interpretation, phobia scoring and emotional reactions).
ai_tool.how_used: Participants prompted FLUX.1 to create images or uploaded their own images. GPT-4o interpreted and scored submissions and generated the selected machine's reactions. Conditions changed rewards, gallery acceptance and emotional feedback; image-generation access was available in all conditions (pp. 3-4, Sections IV.B-E).

task.description: Create or upload images intended to frighten a machine with an assigned phobia, submit them for scoring, and iteratively try further images. Successful artifacts entered a public gallery visible to later users (pp. 3-4, Sections IV.A-E).

outcomes.name: Prompt predictability from preceding submissions (GPT-2 contextual log-likelihood delta)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: For each prompt, GPT-2 log-likelihood with the 20 immediately preceding prompts to the same machine as semicolon-separated context minus log-likelihood for the prompt in isolation. Higher values mean greater predictability from prior submissions and more repetition (p. 11, Appendix E.B). Predictability is regressed on prompt order (p. 4, Section IV.F.2). Figure 5 shows binned means with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals and linear regression with 95% confidence bands (p. 6). Robustness variants use gallery-visible accepted prompts as context with all submissions as targets (amplified divergence), or gallery-visible context with accepted submissions only (same trend, reduced statistical power; p. 11, Appendix B; p. 13, Figure 8). The measure captures surface-text repetition and does not establish conceptual breadth (p. 6, continuation of Section V.B).

contrasts.reported: Combined scoring versus spookiness-only scoring: prompt predictability increased for spookiness-only machines (b = 0.0075 per prompt, p < .001) but showed no trend for combined machines (b = 0.0004, p = .776). Between-condition difference: early prompts 1-30, p = .689; late prompts 31-70, d = 0.611, p = .012. Higher contextual log-likelihood delta indicates more repetition/convergence; the reported positive d is retained without sign conversion. The score compares each prompt with and without the preceding 20 prompts to the same machine as context. The authors caution that it measures surface-text repetition, not validated conceptual breadth.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section V.B (slopes and early/late contrasts); p. 6, Figure 5 and continuation of Section V.B (direction and interpretation caveat); p. 11, Appendix E.B (measure definition).

diversity_detail.metric: Contextual minus isolated prompt log-likelihood; larger deltas indicate more convergence.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Not applicable: GPT-2 is the likelihood scoring model, not an embedding model.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each prompt against the preceding 20 prompts submitted to the same machine; gallery-visible context and accepted-target variants are described in measure_detail.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Regression on prompt order; Figure 5 reports binned means with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals and linear regression with 95% confidence bands. Numerical interval bounds and slope standard errors are not printed (pp. 4-6, Sections IV.F.2 and V.B, Figure 5).
diversity_detail.notes: Lower predictability corresponds to less repetition. The positive reported d is preserved as printed, without computing a sign conversion. This metric is independent of the embedding space used for rewards and cannot distinguish conceptual breadth from surface variation within a theme (pp. 4 and 6).

outcomes.name: Raw phobia score (GPT-4o-rated fear relevance of each artifact)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-4o adopts the selected machine's phobia and rates how strongly an artifact triggers it on a 0-100 scale. This is the raw score, distinct from the refined spookiness score. It is a model-assigned fear-relevance proxy, not an independently validated creativity measure (p. 3, Section IV.C; p. 4, Section IV.F; p. 15, Appendix G.B). The time trajectory uses a mixed-effects model with a machine random intercept (p. 4, Section IV.F.1).

contrasts.reported: Combined scoring versus spookiness-only scoring: raw phobia scores did not differ (d = 0.05, n.s.). GPT-4o scores how strongly the artifact triggers the machine's phobia on a 0-100 scale. This is a task-effectiveness proxy for creative output, not an independently validated creativity rating.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section V.B, opening paragraph (d and nonsignificance); p. 3, Section IV.C (scoring); p. 4, Section IV.F (proxy limitation).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Later prompt windows for a machine
contrasts.control_arm: Earlier prompt windows for the same machine
contrasts.reported: Phobia scores increased through the first 30 prompts and then declined toward baseline in later interactions (mixed-effects model, p < .05). Methods specify a machine random intercept. No numerical trajectory coefficient or standard error is reported; this is an observational time trajectory, not an AI-versus-no-AI contrast.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section V.A and Figure 3B; p. 4, Section IV.F.1.

contrasts.reported: High-emotion versus neutral: phobia scores were described as indistinguishable. The paper gives shared bounds across phobia scores, quality, novelty, acceptance rates, engagement volume and depth: all |d| < 0.06 and all p > .05. It does not report a separate exact d or p for this outcome.

outcomes.name: Convergence toward the public gallery (distance of submission embeddings to the gallery centroid)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: L2 distance from each submission embedding to the gallery centroid, defined as the mean embedding of accepted artifacts, in 50-dimensional PCA space over successive attempts. The model is OLS with machine fixed effects and a condition-by-attempt interaction (pp. 4-5, Section IV.F.3). Smaller distances mean greater gallery convergence. The embedding model for this analysis is not separately identified; it is not inferred from the models used for scoring or other diversity analyses.

contrasts.reported: High-emotion versus neutral machines: users with high-emotion machines converged more rapidly toward gallery content (condition-by-attempt interaction, p = .005). The outcome was L2 distance to the centroid of accepted-artifact embeddings in 50-dimensional PCA space, analyzed with OLS and machine fixed effects. No numerical interaction coefficient or standard error is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section V.C (interaction result); pp. 4-5, Section IV.F.3 (distance measure and model).

diversity_detail.metric: L2 distance to the gallery centroid in 50-dimensional PCA space; smaller distances indicate greater convergence.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each successive submission relative to the mean embedding of the accepted artifacts in its machine's gallery (pp. 4-5, Section IV.F.3).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: OLS with machine fixed effects and a condition-by-attempt interaction; interaction p = .005. No numerical interaction coefficient or standard error is reported (pp. 4-5, Section IV.F.3; p. 6, Section V.C).
diversity_detail.notes: The embedding model is not separately specified for this analysis. Gallery viewing was not verified, and emotional condition switched after successful interactions, limiting causal interpretation (p. 7, Section VI).

outcomes.name: Collective semantic diversity of prompts (pairwise cosine distance)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: The main text tracks sliding-window pairwise cosine distances over text-embedding-3-large prompt embeddings with a mixed-effects model and machine random intercept; Figure 3A labels the measure mean pairwise cosine distance. It also compares within-machine, between-machine/same-phobia and between-phobia distances (p. 4, Section IV.F.1; p. 5, Section V.A and Figure 3). Appendix E.A separately describes cumulative minimum-spanning-tree (MST) total cosine-distance edge weight over windows 1-5, 1-10, ..., 1-100, averaged across machines within scoring conditions (p. 11). The MST method is distinct from mean pairwise distance; the main-text p-values are not reassigned to MST and no numerical MST effect is stated.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Later prompt windows for a machine
contrasts.control_arm: Earlier prompt windows for the same machine
contrasts.reported: Semantic diversity declined over time (mixed-effects model, p < .001). Methods specify a machine random intercept. No numerical coefficient or standard error is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section V.A and Figure 3A; p. 4, Section IV.F.1.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Pairs of prompts within the same machine
contrasts.control_arm: Pairs from different machines sharing a phobia
contrasts.reported: Within-machine distances were smaller than between-machine distances for the same phobia (Mann-Whitney U, p < .001). The paper reports this bound for both transitions in the distance hierarchy; no numerical U statistic, mean difference or standard error is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section V.A and Figure 3C; p. 4, Section IV.F.1.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Pairs from different machines sharing a phobia
contrasts.control_arm: Pairs from machines with different phobias
contrasts.reported: Between-machine distances for the same phobia were smaller than between-phobia distances (Mann-Whitney U, p < .001). The paper reports this bound for both transitions in the distance hierarchy; no numerical U statistic, mean difference or standard error is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section V.A and Figure 3C; p. 4, Section IV.F.1.

diversity_detail.metric: Main text and Figure 3: mean pairwise cosine distance. Appendix E.A: distinct cumulative MST total cosine-distance edge weight.
diversity_detail.computed_over: The time trajectory uses sets of prompts in sliding windows within each machine. The distance hierarchy compares embedding pairs within machines, between machines sharing a phobia, and between phobias. The separately described MST method uses cumulative machine-level prompt sets and averages across machines by scoring condition.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Mixed-effects model with a machine random intercept for time trajectories; Mann-Whitney U tests for the distance hierarchy (p. 4, Section IV.F.1; p. 5, Section V.A). Numerical coefficients, test statistics and interval bounds are not printed.
diversity_detail.notes: The unit set describes the window-level diversity trajectory; the hierarchy tests operate on embedding pairs. Neither unit counts people. Pairwise distance and cumulative MST dispersion are preserved as distinct methods; their relationship is not explained in the document (p. 11, Appendix E.A).

outcomes.name: Refined spookiness score (task-effectiveness proxy)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The raw GPT-4o phobia score is combined with kernel-regression estimates from semantically similar prior artifacts and a prior, yielding a posterior mean that is rescaled into the spookiness score. Artifact interpretations use text-embedding-3-small for neighbor retrieval (pp. 11-13, Appendix F.A-D). This is a model-based task-effectiveness proxy. For accepted-artifact scoring comparisons, methods specify Cohen's d and bootstrap confidence intervals across machines (p. 4, Section IV.F.2); numerical interval bounds are not printed.

contrasts.reported: Among accepted artifacts, combined versus spookiness-only: M = 57.0 versus 67.9; d = -1.37, p < .0001. Methods name Cohen's d and bootstrap confidence intervals across machines; no numerical confidence limits, SDs or analysis counts are printed for this comparison.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section V.B; p. 6, Figure 4A; p. 4, Section IV.F.2.

contrasts.reported: Within the combined condition, habituated versus accepted artifacts: M = 68.5 versus 57.0; d = 1.65, p < .0001. This compares artifact categories within one scoring condition, not randomized groups of people. The Results explicitly label this as spookiness, whereas the corresponding Methods sentence refers to phobia scores.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section V.B (spookiness result); p. 4, Section IV.F.2 (methods wording).

outcomes.name: Uncertainty score (model-derived novelty proxy)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The scoring algorithm interprets the posterior standard error of the mean as uncertainty about an artifact relative to prior artifacts, then rescales and caps it. Underexplored semantic regions or scores diverging from neighbors receive higher uncertainty. Artifact interpretations use text-embedding-3-small for neighbor retrieval. This is a model-derived novelty proxy, not an independently validated human originality rating (p. 4, Section IV.C; pp. 11-13, Appendix F.A-D). Methods specify Cohen's d and bootstrap confidence intervals across machines for accepted-artifact scoring comparisons (p. 4, Section IV.F.2).

contrasts.reported: Among accepted artifacts, combined versus spookiness-only: M = 35.1 versus 15.5; d = 2.0, p < .0001. Methods name Cohen's d and bootstrap confidence intervals across machines; no numerical confidence limits, SDs or analysis counts are printed for this comparison.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section V.B; p. 6, Figure 4B; p. 4, Section IV.F.2.

outcomes.name: Artifact acceptance into the public gallery (scored task success)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: An artifact is accepted when its condition-specific composite score reaches the machine's threshold and moderation does not veto the trigger. Thus acceptance is a score-based success outcome for the artifact (p. 4, Section IV.C; p. 14, Appendix F.E-G). Rates over successive user attempts are analyzed with a logistic mixed-effects model including a condition-by-attempt interaction (p. 4, Section IV.F.2). Percentages are acceptance rates, not person counts.

contrasts.reported: Combined versus spookiness-only: first-attempt acceptance 38% versus 32%; fifth-attempt acceptance 32% versus 40%. Condition-by-attempt interaction p = .004 (logistic mixed-effects model). No numerical interaction coefficient or standard error is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section V.B; p. 6, Figure 4C; p. 4, Section IV.F.2.

contrasts.reported: High-emotion versus neutral: acceptance rates were described as indistinguishable. The paper gives shared bounds across phobia scores, quality, novelty, acceptance rates, engagement volume and depth: all |d| < 0.06 and all p > .05. It does not report a separate exact d or p for this outcome.

contrasts.reported: High-emotion versus neutral: quality measures were described as indistinguishable. The paper gives shared bounds across phobia scores, quality, novelty, acceptance rates, engagement volume and depth: all |d| < 0.06 and all p > .05. It is retained under its printed label rather than assumed to be identical to the uncertainty score. The paper gives shared bounds across phobia scores, quality, novelty, acceptance rates, engagement volume and depth: all |d| < 0.06 and all p > .05. It does not report a separate exact d or p for this outcome.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is not met: participants selected machines and could generate or upload images (p. 3, Section IV.C). Scoring-rule randomization applies to machines (p. 13, Appendix F.D), and emotional condition flips after five successful scares (p. 3, Section IV.B; p. 7, Section VI). Random assignment of people or within-person condition order is not documented. Generative image tools were offered across configurations, so the design is observational rather than quasi_people as defined in form-spec.md. Criterion 2 remains unclear: the reported 832 unique participants are a deployment count; neither the final distinct-person analysis count after record exclusions nor per-arm people counts are reported (p. 4, Sections IV.E-F; supplement pp. 11-18). Criterion 3 is met by output-based fear-relevance, novelty-proxy, task-success and prompt-diversity measures (pp. 4-6, Sections IV.F and V). The added outcomes do not change exclusion from the core or retention as observational context.

one_line_finding: With participant-selected machines, combined spookiness-and-novelty rewards were associated with less late-stage prompt repetition than spookiness-only rewards (reported d = 0.611, p = .012), while raw phobia scores did not differ (d = 0.05, n.s.; p. 5, Section V.B).
notes: The emotional-condition summary labels quality and novelty without explicitly identifying their metrics. S1-O8 and S1-O9 preserve those labels and shared bounds with unknown measure and analysis unit set to null; they may overlap S1-O5 and S1-O6 and must not be treated as additional independent effects. The shared emotional-condition bounds also cover engagement volume and depth, which are not coded as creative-output outcomes here (p. 6, Section V.C). The main pairwise-distance measure and the separately described cumulative MST method remain distinct (p. 5, Figure 3; p. 11, Appendix E.A). AI availability describes the offered image-generation tool across configurations; actual submissions could also be uploaded images (p. 3, Section IV.C).
